mainTopic: Who may permit a בכור or dissolve a נדר; refunds for forbidden food sold by mistake; and the start of the פרק on blemishes of a בכור
overview: The גמרא finishes רב חייא בר עמרם's rulings. Three regular people may permit a בכור where there is no expert, against רבי יוסי, and three may dissolve a נדר where there is no חכם, against רבי יהודה. It explains who counts as a real חכם and what the other judges need to know. רב rules that the הלכה is not like רבי יוסי. The גמרא tries to use this to prove the earlier ruling came from שמואל, but that proof is pushed away. A new משנה teaches what happens when a seller sells a בכור never shown to an expert, or meat that turns out to be טרפה. A ברייתא adds טבל and יין נסך, and רבי שמעון בן אלעזר says the seller may deduct for foods the buyer enjoyed. The גמרא explains that the seller really lost value in each case. The פרק כל פסולי המוקדשין then closes. A new פרק opens with ear blemishes that permit a בכור, and the גמרא begins deriving which blemishes count from the כלל ופרט וכלל in the פסוק. Its question about hidden blemishes continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Two rulings, each rejecting a different תנא
steps.stepSummary: The ruling that three may permit a בכור rejects רבי יוסי. A second ruling says three may dissolve a נדר where there is no חכם, which rejects רבי יהודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: The first ruling comes to exclude רבי יוסי. Also, three people may dissolve a vow in a place with no Sage, which excludes רבי יהודה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes a ruling begun on the previous דף and adds a second, parallel ruling about dissolving vows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first ruling lets three regular people permit a blemished בכור. That goes against רבי יוסי in the משנה, who demands an expert. The second ruling uses the same pattern for vows: three regular people are enough, which goes against רבי יהודה.

keyTerms.meaning: to exclude; this ruling comes to reject someone's opinion
a Sage, a recognized Torah scholar

phrases.english: to exclude the view of Rabbi Yosei.
phrases.notes: This finishes the ruling from the previous דף: three regular people may permit a בכור where no expert is around.

phrases.english: Three may dissolve a vow
in a place where there is no Sage,
to exclude the view of Rabbi Yehuda,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues רב חייא בר עמרם's ruling from the previous דף.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Three regular people may permit a בכור where there is no expert, against רבי יוסי. Three may dissolve a נדר where there is no חכם, against רבי יהודה.

steps.title: The ברייתא showing רבי יהודה's opinion
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא shows that רבי יהודה requires one of the three to be a חכם.
steps.simpleTranslation: As we learned: dissolving vows needs three people. רבי יהודה says one of them must be a Sage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to show which opinion of רבי יהודה the ruling is rejecting.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תנא קמא says any three people can dissolve a vow. רבי יהודה adds that one of the three must be a חכם. So the ruling that three regular people are enough rejects רבי יהודה.

phrases.english: as it is taught in a baraita:
Dissolving vows is done by three;

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: אֶחָד מֵהֶם חָכָם.
phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says: one of them must be a Sage.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source for the opinion that step 1 says is rejected.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי יהודה requires a חכם among the three

steps.title: Who counts as a real Sage?
steps.stepSummary: The ruling mentioned 'a place where there is no חכם,' so the גמרא asks who counts as such a חכם.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'In a place where there is no Sage.' For example, who?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what level of scholar is meant by a חכם who could dissolve a vow alone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ruling suggests that where a real חכם is present, he dissolves the vow and three regular people are not used. So we need to know who qualifies as that kind of חכם.

phrases.english: 'In a place where there is no Sage.'
For example, who?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Clarifies a phrase from step 1.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What kind of scholar counts as the חכם mentioned in the ruling

steps.title: רב נחמן: someone like me
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן says a חכם means a scholar of his own standing.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said: for example, someone like me.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן answers that the חכם meant here is a leading scholar on his level.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An ordinary learned person is not enough. Only a top expert can dissolve a vow alone. Where no one like that is available, three people are used.

phrases.english: Rav Naḥman said:
For example, someone like me.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 3.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A חכם is a top-level scholar like רב נחמן.

steps.title: Can the other two judges be anyone at all?
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה said one of the three must be a חכם. Does that mean the other two can be anyone, even people with no knowledge?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה says one of them must be a Sage. Does that imply the others can be anybody?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws a possible inference from רבי יהודה's words and asks whether it is correct.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Requiring only one חכם seems to mean the other two need no qualifications at all. The גמרא checks whether that is really so.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: אֶחָד מֵהֶן חָכָם,
phrases.english: 'Rabbi Yehuda says: one of them must be a Sage.'
Does that imply that those others can be anyone?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the ברייתא in step 2 to clarify it.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What qualifications the other two members need

steps.title: רבינא: they must be able to understand
steps.stepSummary: רבינא explains that the other two must be people who can understand the laws of vows when they are explained to them.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: people to whom it is explained, and they understand.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא answers that the others need not be experts, but they cannot be completely ignorant.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The other two do not need to know the laws on their own. They must be able to follow and understand when the laws are explained. This is a middle level between a חכם and 'anyone.'

keyTerms.meaning: that it is explained to him

phrases.english: Ravina said:
They must be people to whom it is explained, and who understand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 5.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The other two must be able to understand the laws when they are explained.
steps.whatToRemember: A real חכם is someone on the level of רב נחמן. Under רבי יהודה, the other two judges must at least be able to understand explanations.

steps.title: רב: the הלכה is not like רבי יוסי
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes רבי יוסי's view in the משנה, and רב rules that the הלכה does not follow him.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי says: even if there are twenty-three there, and so on. רב חננאל said in the name of רב: the הלכה is not like רבי יוסי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the משנה and brings רב's ruling against רבי יוסי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוסי holds that even a court of twenty-three cannot permit a בכור; only an expert can. רב rules that we do not follow רבי יוסי.

keyTerms.meaning: twenty-three, the size of a בית דין for capital cases
etc.; the quote continues as in the משנה
the הלכה is not (like this view)

phrases.english: 'Rabbi Yosei says:

phrases.aramaic: אֲפִילּוּ יֵשׁ שָׁם עֶשְׂרִים וּשְׁלֹשָׁה כּוּ׳.
phrases.english: even if there are twenty-three there,' and so on.
Rav Ḥananel said in the name of Rav:
The halacha is not like Rabbi Yosei.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חֲנַנְאֵל אָמַר רַב אֵין הֲלָכָה כְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next line of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The הלכה is not like רבי יוסי.

steps.title: Isn't this obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רב needed to say this, since the הלכה always follows the majority over a lone opinion.
steps.simpleTranslation: That is obvious! When it is one against many, the הלכה follows the many.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב's ruling as unnecessary.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוסי stands alone against the חכמים. The general rule already tells us to follow the majority, so רב's statement seems to add nothing.

phrases.english: It is obvious!
With an individual against the many, the halacha follows the many!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the need for רב's ruling.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's ruling that the הלכה is not like רבי יוסי
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The majority rule already decides this, so the ruling seems unnecessary.

steps.title: His reasoning might have been followed
steps.stepSummary: Without רב, we might have said רבי יוסי is an exception because his reasoning is especially strong. רב teaches that he is not.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said his reasoning is with him. So רב teaches us otherwise.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why רב's ruling was needed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a known idea that רבי יוסי's opinions are well reasoned and sometimes followed even against others. So we might have followed him here. רב tells us that here, too, the majority rule applies.

keyTerms.meaning: his reasoning is with him; his logic is sound

phrases.english: You might have said
that his reasoning is with him,
phrases.notes: Meaning רבי יוסי's opinions are carefully reasoned, so we might follow him even when he stands alone.

phrases.english: so it teaches us that we do not.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 8.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows the ruling was needed to block a mistaken assumption
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We might have followed רבי יוסי because נימוקו עמו.
steps.terutzMaskana: The majority rule applies; the הלכה is not like רבי יוסי.

steps.title: So the earlier ruling came from שמואל
steps.stepSummary: Since רב himself ruled against רבי יוסי, the earlier ruling, whose author was uncertain, must have come from שמואל.
steps.simpleTranslation: Resolve the question from this: that earlier ruling was said in the name of שמואל. If it were in the name of רב, why would I need two rulings?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא uses רב's ruling to settle the earlier doubt about whether the first ruling was said in the name of רב or שמואל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both rulings say the same thing: we do not follow רבי יוסי. If רב had said both, one would be extra. So the first one must have been said in the name of שמואל.

phrases.english: Resolve the question from this:
that the first one
was said in the name of Shmuel.
For if it were in the name of Rav,
why would I need two?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses רב's ruling from step 7 to settle the earlier doubt behind step 1.
steps.raayaObject: That the first ruling was said in the name of שמואל
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב's own ruling against רבי יוסי, which would make a second ruling from רב unnecessary
steps.whatToRemember: If רב had said both rulings, one would be extra, so the first ruling is credited to שמואל.

steps.title: Maybe only one ruling was really said
steps.stepSummary: The proof that the earlier ruling came from שמואל is rejected. רב may have said only one ruling, and the other was inferred from it.
steps.simpleTranslation: One ruling was said as an inference from the other.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the proof from step 10. רב did not necessarily say two separate rulings. He may have said one, and his students worked out the other from it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof in step 10 assumed that רב would not repeat himself, so the earlier ruling must belong to שמואל. This step removes that assumption: if רב said only one ruling and the other was inferred from it, both can still be רב's. So the question of who said the earlier ruling stays open.

keyTerms.meaning: By inference; drawn out from something else that was said

steps.whatToRemember: The proof that the ruling came from שמואל falls away. One of רב's rulings may simply have been inferred from the other.

phrases.english: One ruling, by inference
phrases.notes: The word in round brackets is the printed text; the word in square brackets is the corrected reading. Both mean the same thing.

phrases.english: from the other one, was stated.
phrases.notes: He means that רב said only one ruling, and people worked out the second one from it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof given in step 10
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof that the uncertain ruling must have come from שמואל
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: It assumed רב said two separate rulings. He may have said only one, and the other was inferred from it.

steps.title: A firstborn sold without being shown to an expert
steps.stepSummary: The new משנה: if someone slaughters and sells a בכור without showing it to an expert, he refunds all the money, and any meat left over is buried.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone slaughters a firstborn animal and it then becomes known that he did not show it to an expert: what the buyers ate, they ate, and he must return the money to them. What they did not eat must be buried, and he must return the money.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It deals with a seller who sold meat from a בכור without first having an expert check its blemish.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The buyers did nothing wrong, so they do not pay for meat they already ate. The seller refunds the full price, even for that eaten meat. Any meat that is left is not given back to him; it must be buried, because it is forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: The משנה; marks the start of the משנה text
A firstborn male animal, which may be eaten only if it has a blemish confirmed by an expert
Money; the price that was paid

phrases.english: MISHNA: One who slaughters the firstborn animal,
and it became known that he did not show it —
phrases.notes: He means that he did not show the animal's blemish to an expert before slaughtering it.

phrases.english: what they ate, they ate,
and he must return the money to them,
and what they did not eat —
the meat must be buried,
and he must return the money.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ הַשּׁוֹחֵט אֶת הַבְּכוֹר וְנוֹדַע שֶׁלֹּא הֶרְאָהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new משנה on a new topic
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The seller refunds the full price, even for meat already eaten. Leftover meat is buried.

steps.title: A cow sold and then found to be a טרפה
steps.stepSummary: The משנה's second case: the leftover meat of a טרפה cow goes back to the seller, and he refunds the money. If the buyers already sold it to non-Jews or fed it to dogs, they pay what טרפה meat is worth.
steps.simpleTranslation: Likewise, if someone slaughters a cow and sells it, and it becomes known that it is a טרפה: what the buyers ate, they ate. What they did not eat, they return the meat to him, and he returns the money to them. If they sold it to non-Jews or threw it to dogs, they pay the value of טרפה meat.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives a similar case: meat sold as kosher that turns out to be a טרפה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Unlike the בכור, a טרפה may still be used in other ways, so it is not buried. Instead the meat goes back to the seller. If the buyers already got some use out of it by selling it or feeding dogs, they pay its lower value as טרפה meat, and the seller refunds the rest.

keyTerms.meaning: An animal with a fatal defect, forbidden to eat but allowed for other uses
They threw it to the dogs

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two cases. The בכור meat is buried because no one may benefit from it. The טרפה meat is returned because it can still be sold to non-Jews.

phrases.english: And likewise, one who slaughters a cow and sells it,
and it becomes known that it is treif —
what they ate, they ate,
and what they did not eat —
they return the meat to him,
and he returns the money to them.
If they sold it to non-Jews,
or threw it to the dogs —
they pay the value of treif meat.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכֵן הַשּׁוֹחֵט אֶת הַפָּרָה וּמְכָרָהּ וְנוֹדַע שֶׁהִיא טְרֵפָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Second case of the same משנה, parallel to the בכור case
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Leftover טרפה meat goes back to the seller, who refunds the money. Buyers who already used the meat pay what טרפה meat is worth.
steps.whatToRemember: בכור meat is buried and fully refunded. טרפה meat is returned to the seller, or paid for at the טרפה price if the buyers already used it.

steps.title: A ברייתא: forbidden meat, produce, or wine
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches the same refund rule for בכור meat, טבל produce, and יין נסך: the buyers keep what they ate, and the seller refunds all the money.
steps.simpleTranslation: The חכמים taught: If someone sells meat to his friend and it turns out to be בכור meat, or produce that turns out to be טבל, or wine that turns out to be יין נסך: what they ate, they ate, and he must return the money to them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins by quoting a ברייתא that extends the משנה's rule to more kinds of forbidden food.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה spoke only about meat. The ברייתא adds produce that was never tithed and wine used for idol worship. In all of these cases the seller refunds the full price, even for what the buyers already ate.

keyTerms.meaning: Produce from which the required tithes were not yet taken
Wine poured for idol worship, forbidden to drink or benefit from

phrases.english: GEMARA: The Rabbis taught:
One who sells meat to his fellow
and it was found to be meat of a firstborn,
produce, and it was found to be untithed,
wine, and it was found to be idolatrous libation wine —
what they ate, they ate,
and he must return the money to them.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן הַמּוֹכֵר בָּשָׂר לַחֲבֵירוֹ וְנִמְצָא בְּשַׂר בְּכוֹר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a ברייתא that widens the rule of the משנה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: For בכור meat, טבל, or יין נסך, the buyers keep what they ate and the seller refunds the full price.

steps.title: Disgusting foods get a full refund, enjoyable foods get a partial refund
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר qualifies the refund rule. For foods people find disgusting, the seller refunds all the money. For foods people do not find disgusting, he subtracts the value of what was eaten.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר says: for items people are disgusted by, the seller returns all the money. For items people are not disgusted by, he subtracts some of the money. The disgusting items are נבילות, טריפות, שקצים and רמשים. The items people are not disgusted by are בכורות, טבלים and יין נסך.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא from Step 14 continues with רבי שמעון בן אלעזר, who adds a distinction to the refund rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first opinion said the seller always refunds everything. רבי שמעון בן אלעזר says that depends on whether the buyer enjoyed the food. If the food is disgusting, the buyer got no pleasure from it, so he gets a full refund. If it is normal tasty food, the buyer did benefit, so the seller may deduct that value.

keyTerms.meaning: a person is disgusted by it
animals that died without proper שחיטה

steps.confusionAlert: The list of 'not disgusting' items does not mean they are permitted. בכור, טבל and יין נסך are still forbidden to the buyer. The point is only that eating them is enjoyable, so the buyer got real benefit.

phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says:
Items that a person is disgusted by
he must return all the money to them,
and items that a person is not disgusted by
he deducts from the money for them.
phrases.notes: He takes off the value of what they enjoyed eating and returns the rest.

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵלּוּ הֵן דְּבָרִים שֶׁהַנֶּפֶשׁ קָצָה בָּהֶן:
phrases.english: And these are the items a person is disgusted by:
animal carcasses and treif animals, repulsive creatures and creeping things.

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵלּוּ הֵן דְּבָרִים שֶׁאֵין הַנֶּפֶשׁ קָצָה בָּהֶן:
phrases.english: And these are the items a person is not disgusted by:
firstborn animals, untithed produce, and wine poured for idols.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a dissenting distinction to the ברייתא's refund rule in Step 14.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Disgusting forbidden foods get a full refund. Enjoyable forbidden foods get a refund minus the value of what was eaten.

steps.title: Why can the seller charge for a בכור he could never use?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges deducting for בכור meat: the buyer can say he caused the seller no loss, since the seller could never have eaten it anyway.
steps.simpleTranslation: About a בכור: let the buyer say to the seller, 'What loss did I cause you?'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי שמעון בן אלעזר's rule that the seller may deduct money for the בכור meat the buyer ate.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An unblemished בכור is forbidden to the seller too. So the meat was worthless to him, and the buyer eating it took nothing of value from him. Why should the buyer pay anything for it?

keyTerms.meaning: but let him say to him

phrases.english: A firstborn animal:
but let the buyer say to him: What loss did I cause you?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the inclusion of בכור in the 'deduct' category of Step 15.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר's ruling that the seller deducts for בכור meat.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The seller had no right to eat the בכור, so the buyer caused him no loss and should owe nothing.

steps.title: The בכור had a blemish and could have been permitted
steps.stepSummary: The ruling is about meat sold from a בכור that had a blemish. The seller could have shown it to an expert even after slaughter and gotten it permitted, following רבי יהודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, the ruling is needed for a case where he sold him meat from a blemished animal. The seller can say: if you hadn't eaten it, I would have shown it to an expert and he would have permitted it to me. This follows רבי יהודה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by placing the case where the בכור had a real blemish, so the seller did lose something.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A blemished בכור may be eaten once an expert examines it. רבי יהודה holds that this examination can happen even after slaughter. So the meat was really permittable for the seller, and by eating it the buyer destroyed something of value.

keyTerms.meaning: no, it is needed for a specific case
I would have shown it to an expert

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the deduction depends on the seller really losing something. That idea explains the טבל and יין נסך cases in the next step too.

phrases.english: No, it is needed
for a case where he sold him meat from the place of a blemish,
phrases.notes: The animal had a blemish, but no expert had looked at it yet.

phrases.english: so the seller says to him:
If you had not eaten it,
I would have shown it to an expert and he would have permitted it to me,
in line with Rabbi Yehuda.
phrases.notes: רבי יהודה holds a בכור can be examined for a blemish even after it was slaughtered.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא צְרִיכָא, כְּגוֹן דְּזַבֵּין לֵיהּ מִמְּקוֹם מוּמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 16 by narrowing the case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case (אוקימתא) to a blemished בכור, following one opinion.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The בכור was worthless to the seller, so the buyer owes nothing.
steps.terutzMaskana: The בכור was blemished and could have been permitted after slaughter, so the seller lost real value.

steps.title: The seller also lost value with טבל and יין נסך
steps.stepSummary: The same reasoning covers the other items. טבל could have been tithed and eaten, and יין נסך was mixed into permitted wine, following רבן שמעון בן גמליאל.
steps.simpleTranslation: With טבלים, the seller says: I would have fixed them and eaten them. With יין נסך, the case is where it was mixed with other wine, following רבן שמעון בן גמליאל.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא applies the same answer to the other two 'not disgusting' items, explaining how the seller lost something with each one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: טבל is only forbidden until its tithes are separated, so the seller could have fixed it and eaten it. יין נסך by itself is fully forbidden. So the case must be where it was mixed into permitted wine, which רבן שמעון בן גמליאל allows the owner to benefit from. In both cases the buyer ate something that had real value to the seller.

keyTerms.meaning: I would fix it (separate the tithes)

steps.whatToRemember: Under רבי שמעון בן אלעזר, the seller deducts only when the buyer enjoyed the food and also took something the seller could really have used: a blemished בכור, fixable טבל, or יין נסך mixed into permitted wine.

phrases.english: Untithed produce:
I would have fixed them and eaten them,
phrases.notes: 'Fixed' means separating the תרומות and מעשרות, which makes the produce permitted.

phrases.english: Wine poured for idols:
the case is where it was in a mixture,
and in line with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

steps.triggerLanguage: טְבָלִים הֲוָה מַתְקֵינְנָא לְהוּ וְאָכֵלְנָא לְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends the answer of Step 17 to the other two items in רבי שמעון בן אלעזר's list.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Showing that each item had real value to the seller, and limiting the יין נסך case to a mixture.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: טבל and יין נסך are forbidden, so the seller lost nothing when the buyer ate them.
steps.terutzMaskana: טבל could have been tithed, and mixed יין נסך could have been used under רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, so the seller lost real value.

steps.title: The source for רבן שמעון בן גמליאל on mixed forbidden wine
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a משנה: when יין נסך falls into a cistern, the חכמים forbid all the wine. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל lets it all be sold to non-Jews, except for the value of the forbidden wine.
steps.simpleTranslation: As we learned in a משנה: If יין נסך fell into a wine cistern, all of the wine is forbidden for any benefit. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: All of it may be sold to non-Jews, except for the value of the יין נסך that is in it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the משנה that backs up the previous step, where it relied on רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's view about mixed wine.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, the mixed wine still has value, because it can be sold to non-Jews for money. That is why the seller lost something real when the buyers drank it. So it makes sense to subtract the value of what they drank from the refund.

keyTerms.meaning: A cistern or pit for storing wine
Forbidden for any benefit, not only for eating or drinking

steps.whatToRemember: The deduction rule of רבי שמעון בן אלעזר works even for יין נסך. According to רבן שמעון בן גמליאל a mixed cistern can still be sold, so the wine had value to the seller.

phrases.english: As we learned: Libation wine that fell into a cistern —
phrases.notes: This משנה is in מסכת עבודה זרה.

phrases.english: all of it is forbidden for benefit.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
All of it may be sold to non-Jews,
except for the value of the libation wine that is in it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Provides the source for the view of רבן שמעון בן גמליאל cited in step 18.
steps.raayaObject: The claim in step 18 that mixed יין נסך still had value for the seller
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה in עבודה זרה where רבן שמעון בן גמליאל permits selling the whole cistern minus the value of the forbidden wine

steps.title: Hadran — Closing the פרק כל פסולי המוקדשין
steps.stepSummary: The פרק כל פסולי המוקדשין ends with the traditional closing line.
steps.simpleTranslation: We will return to you, פרק כל פסולי המוקדשין.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the standard closing line that marks the end of the פרק. It is not part of the argument.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The הדרן formula expresses our wish to come back and learn this פרק again. After this line, a brand-new topic begins with a new משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: We will return to you, the traditional closing of a פרק
Sacrificial animals that became disqualified, the name of the פרק being closed

phrases.english: We will return to you, "All disqualified consecrated animals."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the perek after the final source in step 19.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The פרק כל פסולי המוקדשין is complete.

steps.title: New פרק: ear blemishes that allow slaughtering a firstborn
steps.stepSummary: The משנה lists ear blemishes that permit slaughtering a בכור: a damaged cartilage, a split, a hole the size of a vetch bean, or a dried-out ear. It also records two views on what counts as dried out.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: For these blemishes one may slaughter a בכור: if its ear was damaged and missing part of the cartilage, but not if only the skin was damaged; if the ear was split, even though nothing is missing; if it was pierced with a hole the size of a vetch bean; or if it dried out. What counts as dried out? Any ear that does not let out a drop of blood when it is pierced. רבי יוסי בן המשולם says: Dried out means it is so dry that it crumbles.
steps.whatsHappening: A new פרק opens with a משנה that lists specific ear blemishes which allow a בכור to be slaughtered and eaten outside the מקדש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Damage to the cartilage counts, but damage to the skin alone does not. A split counts even if nothing is missing, and a hole needs to be at least the size of a vetch bean. For a dried-out ear, the תנא קמא's test is that it does not bleed when pierced, while רבי יוסי בן המשולם requires that it be dry enough to crumble.

keyTerms.meaning: Blemishes or physical defects in an animal
Cartilage, the firm part of the ear
Bitter vetch, a small bean used as a size measure

steps.confusionAlert: Damage that is only in the skin of the ear is not a blemish. It has to reach the cartilage.

phrases.english: MISHNA: For these blemishes
one may slaughter the firstborn:
phrases.notes: He means slaughtering it outside the מקדש and eating it, since a blemished בכור cannot be brought as a קרבן.

phrases.english: its ear was damaged from the cartilage,
but not the skin,

phrases.aramaic: נִסְדְּקָה אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁלֹּא חָסְרָה,
phrases.english: it was split, even though it is not missing anything,
it was pierced the size of a vetch bean,
or it dried out.
What is a dried-out ear?

phrases.aramaic: כֹּל שֶׁתִּנָּקֵב וְאֵינָהּ מוֹצִיאָה טִיפַּת דָּם.
phrases.english: Any ear that, when pierced, does not let out a drop of blood.
Rabbi Yosei ben HaMeshullam says:
Dried out means that it crumbles.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ עַל אֵלּוּ מוּמִין שׁוֹחֲטִין אֶת הַבְּכוֹר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the new perek after the הדרן in step 20.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Ear blemishes that permit slaughtering a בכור: damage to the cartilage but not only the skin, a split, a vetch-sized hole, or a dried-out ear. They disagree on whether dried out means it does not bleed or that it crumbles.

steps.title: Why do these blemishes count if the פסוק only says lame and blind?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why ear blemishes permit slaughtering a בכור, since the פסוק only mentions a lame or blind animal.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: Why? The פסוק says "lame" and "blind"!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the משנה: the תורה names only lameness and blindness, so how can ear blemishes also allow slaughtering a בכור?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק that allows eating a blemished בכור names specific defects, lame and blind. That suggests only defects like those count, so the משנה's list of ear blemishes seems to go beyond the פסוק. The גמרא needs to show where these other blemishes come from.

phrases.english: GEMARA: Why?
"Lame" and "blind" is written!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the basis of the משנה's list of blemishes in step 21.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that ear blemishes permit slaughtering a בכור
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק names only lameness and blindness, which implies that other blemishes, such as ear damage, should not count.

steps.title: The verse also says 'if there be any blemish'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers the question from Step 22 by pointing to the broad phrase 'כִּי יִהְיֶה בוֹ מוּם' in the same פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק also says 'If there be any blemish in it,' so it covers more than lame or blind.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question of why ear blemishes count. The same פסוק has a general phrase, 'any blemish,' and that phrase can include ear blemishes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 22 asked how ear blemishes can count when the פסוק names only lame and blind. The answer is that the פסוק opens with a broad phrase, 'any blemish,' which seems to include every blemish, ears too.

phrases.english: It is also written: 'If there be any blemish in it,'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in Step 22 by pointing to a broader phrase in the same פסוק.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Points to a broader phrase in the source
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Only lame or blind animals count, because only those are named.
steps.terutzMaskana: The general phrase 'any blemish' includes other blemishes, such as ear blemishes.

steps.title: A general followed by a detail limits to the detail
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects: 'any blemish' is a כלל and 'lame or blind' is a פרט, and a כלל followed by a פרט includes only the פרט.
steps.simpleTranslation: But say: 'any blemish' is a general statement and 'lame or blind' is a detail. When a general is followed by a detail, only the detail is included. So lame and blind count, and nothing else does.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer it just gave. It uses a fixed rule for reading פסוקים to argue that the broad phrase is actually limited to lame and blind.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By the rule of כלל ופרט, when a broad term comes first and specific items follow, the broad term covers only those specific items. Read that way, 'any blemish' means only lame or blind. That would put us back at the question of Step 22.

keyTerms.meaning: A general, broad statement in a פסוק
A specific detail in a פסוק
A general followed by a detail: only the detail is included
But say (introduces another way to read)

steps.confusionAlert: In a כלל ופרט, the detail does not add to the general; it limits it. The broad word ends up meaning only the items listed.

phrases.english: But say:
'If there be any blemish in it' is a general statement,
'lame or blind' is a detail,

phrases.aramaic: כְּלָל וּפְרָט אֵין בַּכְּלָל אֶלָּא מָה שֶׁבַּפְּרָט;
phrases.english: and with a general and then a detail, the general includes only what is in the detail;
lame and blind, yes,
anything else, no!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reading in Step 23.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that 'any blemish' includes ear blemishes
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Under the rule of כלל ופרט, the broad term is limited to the listed details, which are lame and blind.

steps.title: A second general makes it general-detail-general
steps.stepSummary: 'כֹּל מוּם רָע' is a second כלל, so the פסוק is a כלל ופרט וכלל. That includes anything like the detail: blemishes that are exposed and do not grow back.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Any ill blemish' generalizes again. With a general, a detail, and a general, you include only things similar to the detail. The detail describes blemishes that are exposed and do not grow back, so all such blemishes count.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. The פסוק ends with another broad phrase, and that changes which rule applies.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When a second כלל follows the פרט, the rule is no longer 'only the detail.' Instead we include anything that shares the features of the detail. Lame and blind are blemishes that are visible and permanent, so any visible, permanent blemish counts.

keyTerms.meaning: It went back and gave a general statement again
General, detail, general: include things similar to the detail
Blemishes that are exposed and visible

steps.whatToRemember: With a כלל ופרט וכלל, we include things like the detail. Lame and blind show that a blemish counts if it is visible and permanent.

phrases.english: 'Any ill blemish': it went back and generalized again,
phrases.notes: This is the end of the same פסוק, דברים 15:21.

phrases.english: so it is a general, a detail, and a general,

phrases.aramaic: אִי אַתָּה דָן אֶלָּא כְּעֵין הַפְּרָט;
phrases.english: and you may derive only things similar to the detail;
just as the detail is clearly spelled out as
blemishes that are exposed and do not grow back,

phrases.aramaic: אַף כֹּל מוּמִין שֶׁבַּגָּלוּי וְאֵינָן חוֹזְרִין.
phrases.english: so too, all blemishes that are exposed and do not grow back.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 24 by showing that the פסוק has a second כלל.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reclassifies the structure of the פסוק
steps.terutzHavaAmina: It is a כלל ופרט, so only lame and blind count.
steps.terutzMaskana: It is a כלל ופרט וכלל, so any exposed, permanent blemish counts.

steps.title: Why not also require that it stops the animal from working?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that lame and blind share a third feature, stopping the animal from working. If that were required, an ear blemish would not count, yet the משנה says it does.
steps.simpleTranslation: But say: the detail describes blemishes that are exposed, stop the animal from working, and do not grow back, so only those count. Why, then, did we learn that an ear damaged in the cartilage, though not in the skin, is a blemish?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the list of features drawn from 'lame or blind.' It proposes a stricter list and shows that the stricter list clashes with our משנה about ears.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Lame and blind animals also cannot do their normal work. If that feature were part of 'similar to the detail,' a damaged ear, which does not stop an animal from working, would not count. The משנה counts it, so the question is why that feature is ignored.

keyTerms.meaning: Stops the animal from doing its normal work
Why, then, did we learn (in the משנה)?
Was damaged and has a piece missing
Cartilage (the firm part of the ear)

phrases.english: But say: just as the detail is clearly spelled out as

phrases.aramaic: מוּמִין שֶׁבַּגָּלוּי, וּבוֹטֵל מִמְּלַאכְתּוֹ, וְאֵינוֹ חוֹזֵר,
phrases.english: blemishes that are exposed, stop the animal from its work, and do not grow back,
so too, all blemishes that are exposed,
stop the animal from its work, and do not grow back.
Why, then, did we learn:
if its ear was damaged in the cartilage,
but not in the skin?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges which features Step 25 draws from the detail.
steps.kashyaTarget: The two-feature definition (exposed and permanent) from Step 25
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The detail has a third feature, stopping work. Requiring it would rule out ear blemishes, which contradicts the משנה.

steps.title: 'Any' is a word that widens
steps.stepSummary: The word 'כֹּל' in 'כֹּל מוּם רָע' widens the category, so the 'stops working' feature is not required.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Any ill blemish' is a widening.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the word 'any' widens what counts, so blemishes that do not stop the animal from working are included too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The extra word 'כֹּל' tells us not to demand every feature of lame and blind. It loosens the 'similar to the detail' test, so an ear blemish counts even though the animal can still work.

keyTerms.meaning: A widening: a word that includes more cases
Any or all (here, the widening word)

phrases.english: 'Any ill blemish' is a widening,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 26.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Points to a widening word in the פסוק
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Only blemishes that stop the animal from working count.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'כֹּל' widens the category, so ear blemishes count even though the animal can still work.

steps.title: Then hidden blemishes should count too
steps.stepSummary: If 'כֹּל' widens so much, hidden blemishes should also count. The גמרא starts to quote a משנה about gums that seems to say otherwise.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, hidden blemishes should count too. Why, then, did we learn: outer gums that were damaged or scratched, and inner gums that were uprooted...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer of Step 27. If the widening has no limit, hidden blemishes should also count, and it begins quoting a משנה about gums to show a problem. The question continues in the next lines.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the 'stops working' feature is dropped, one could ask why the 'exposed' feature should stay. The משנה about gums treats outer gums, which can be seen, differently from inner gums, which are hidden, so the משנה seems to care whether a blemish is visible.

phrases.english: If so, hidden blemishes too?
Why, then, did we learn:
outer gums that were damaged or that were scratched,
and inner gums that were uprooted,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the widening answer of Step 27.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that 'כֹּל' widens the category
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: An unlimited widening would include hidden blemishes too, but the משנה about gums treats outer and inner gums differently, which suggests visibility matters.
